title: What If Your Pool Was 100 Feet Deep? 😱
description:
Gus digs the deepest pool on his street: a hundred feet, straight down. His neighbor says deep water is just more water, so Gus lowers a beach ball to the bottom on a rope, and it comes back with a surprise.

The numbers:
• Fresh water weighs 62.3 lb per cubic foot, so 34 feet of it (33.96 ft) press as hard as the whole atmosphere: 14.7 psi, or 2,116 lb on every square foot.
• At 34 ft the pressure is 2.0 atmospheres, at 100 ft it is 3.95: the air on top plus almost three more.
• Boyle's law: squeezed air shrinks in step with the pressure. A beach ball holds half its volume at 34 ft and a quarter (25.4 %) at 100 ft. A quarter of the volume is 63 % of the width: a 15-inch beach ball becomes a wrinkled 9.5-inch lump, the size of a basketball (9.4 in).
• At the surface that ball pushes up with 64 lb (the weight of the 29 litres of water it pushes aside); a 100 lb iron barbell still weighs 86 lb under water, so it takes the ball down.
• One square foot of the floor carries 100 cubic feet of water: 6,232 lb, a little over three tons.
• The hole: 16 ft x 32 ft x 100 ft = 51,200 cubic feet, about 190 dump-truck loads of 10 cubic yards, and 383,000 gallons of water: 24 days of a garden hose at 11 gallons a minute.
(Assumptions: a 16 x 32 ft pool, fresh water at 20 C, standard air pressure, a 15-inch beach ball, dirt counted as it lies in the ground. A real vinyl ball does not shrink evenly, it crumples; the volume is what the law gives. The pool in the picture is drawn smaller than 16 x 32 ft. Never dive deep on a held breath, and never swim alone.)

Sources:
• NOAA Diving Program, "Atmospheric and Hydrostatic Pressure" and "Boyle's law" (NOAA Diving Manual): 34 ft of fresh water = 14.7 psi = one atmosphere, 0.432 psi per foot; P1V1 = P2V2
• NOAA National Ocean Service, "How does pressure change with ocean depth?": one more atmosphere for every 33 ft of sea water
• NASA Glenn Research Center, "Boyle's Law"
• USGS conversion tables: a cubic foot of water weighs 62.4 lb
• Iowa State University Extension, garden hoses: 100 ft of 5/8-inch hose at 40 psi delivers 11 gallons a minute

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
